overview: Founded in 1347 after a revolt against Delhi, the Bahmani sultanate became a major Deccan power, ruling first from Gulbarga and then Bidar. This map shows only 1500 to 1530, during its fragmentation. Its very narrow southern outline misses both capitals and must not be read as the kingdom’s full territory.

periods.title: A divided kingdom
periods.summary: Mahmud Shah retained the throne while powerful regional rulers controlled much of the former kingdom.

periods.title: Nominal successors
periods.summary: Short reigns followed Mahmud Shah. Sources differ on when the remaining dynasty formally ended.

items.text: Russian merchant Afanasy Nikitin visited the Deccan in the late fifteenth century. His account describes trade in horses, cloth, silk and pepper, and busy trading gatherings. Bidar’s inland court depended on commercial routes reaching the coast, including the port of Dabhol.

Nikitin noticed sharp differences between poor rural people and wealthy nobles carried in silver palanquins, accompanied by horses and attendants. His eye-catching description helps reveal inequality, though a visitor’s contrast does not describe every merchant, craft worker or household in the kingdom.

The kingdom was multilingual: Persian, Marathi, Kannada, Telugu and Dakhni were used in different settings and regions. Court culture connected local families with migrants from Iran, Central Asia and elsewhere. A single royal dynasty did not mean everyone spoke the same language.

Minister Mahmud Gawan ordered land measurements and the fixing of village and town boundaries. These practical surveys helped officials assess revenue. For people cultivating the land, government involved fields, boundaries and tax demands as well as distant ceremonies at court.

When Humayun died in 1461, his young son’s government was entrusted to a regency council that included the queen mother and Mahmud Gawan. Royal women could participate directly in state affairs; this council’s responsibilities went well beyond arranging palace ceremonies.

Yazdani’s history, drawing on earlier chronicles, records schools for orphans at Bidar and other Deccan towns under Muhammad Shah II, who ruled from 1378 to 1397. This is a specific example of organized provision for children, rather than evidence that every child attended school.

Alauddin Ahmad II’s Bidar hospital employed Hindu and Muslim physicians, according to the historical accounts summarized by Yazdani. Endowed land supplied income for medicines, food and drink. Care required a continuing budget, not just a building with an impressive entrance.

Gawan’s madrasa, built at Bidar in 1472, gathered lecture rooms, a prayer hall, a library and living quarters around a large court. Teachers and students could live within the institution. His surviving letters show his efforts to recruit learned people from Iran and Iraq.

The college courtyard contained a twelve-sided cistern. Yazdani thought an underground channel probably supplied it from a well outside the main building. Students’ surroundings therefore combined lessons, residence and a carefully planned water supply: geometry was useful beyond the classroom.

The madrasa’s facade was covered with glazed tiles arranged into flowers and inscriptions in vivid colors. Two minarets originally framed the entrance, although only one survives. Its decoration connected a Deccan school with architectural traditions also seen in Iran and Central Asia.

Gulbarga’s congregational mosque, built in 1367, covered its courtyard rather than leaving the central space open to the sky. Its roofed gathering space is one of the distinctive features noted in India’s heritage submission. The surviving building makes a design choice visible centuries later.

Bidar’s fortifications incorporated gates and sluices that could flood selected portions of the moat while conserving water. Managing defenses required controlling water as well as moving soldiers. The surviving fort also includes later alterations, so every wall should not be assigned to one Bahmani building campaign.

At Ashtur, the royal tombs preserved a different kind of craftsmanship: painted and gilded ceilings inside large domed chambers. These were carefully decorated memorials. Their surviving color helps counter the impression that old stone monuments always looked plain and grey.

sections.title: Stories, money and a written wish

items.text: Bidar attracted musicians, storytellers, dancers and reciters of the Persian Shahnameh, alongside poets and historians. Adhari composed the Bahman-nama, a dynastic history in verse. At court, listening to a story could also mean hearing a carefully shaped account of royal identity.

Bahmani mints produced copper, silver and gold coins carrying Arabic names, titles and dates. Commerce also crossed political borders: Vijayanagara gold coins circulated within Bahmani territories. A market stall did not necessarily require every coin to carry the name of the local ruler.

A silver coin struck at Bidar in 1471 to 1472 for Muhammad Shah III ends its inscription “khallada mulkahu”: “May God preserve the kingdom.” This is the museum catalogue’s Roman transliteration of the original Arabic. A small coin could carry both a ruler’s identity and a prayer.

ending.text: The kingdom fragmented into Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur and Golconda. Nominal Bahmani rulers lingered: Iranica ends the dynasty in 1528, while the Met uses 1538. Neither makes 1530 a secure single fall date. Successor courts continued Deccan artistic and intellectual traditions.
